extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and experimentalists learning principles of measurement error and statistical treatment of observations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the logical origin, verification, and practical treatment of observational errors: when to use the general Law of Error (normal law), how to compute probable errors and means, when to reject or correct observations, and how to apply the method of least squares for multiple unknowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Error (general normal law assumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume an infinite number of infinitely small independent errors acting in either direction; the resulting general law of error is expressed by the formula y = Y e^{-c x^2} (Gaussian-type curve), where x is error amount, Y the maximum ordinate, and c a series-specific constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons for adopting this hypothesis: (1) there may be infinitely numerous causes of error; (2) a moderate finite-number hypothesis gives a law not appreciably different; (3) hypothesis of infinity yields a general, readily calculable law applicable uniformly; (4) empirical series verify the law closely. The continuous law is an approximation (permits arbitrarily large errors with negligible probability). Use when sources of error are unknown ('in the dark').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Arithmetical Triangle when chief error sources known
rubrics_metrics.description: If the observer knows the number and magnitude of chief distinct causes of error, one ought to calculate the special Law of Error from the Arithmetical (Pascal's) Triangle / combinatorial counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: with four independent ±1-inch causes, counts of combinations give frequencies of total errors (1 way for 0 errors, 4 ways for ±1, 6 ways for ±2, etc.). From such numbers compute exact probabilities or cumulative probabilities (illustrated with denominators like 16 or 1024). Use this special law for cases where source counts/magnitudes are known rather than the general continuous law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability of an error within limits equals area under curve
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability that the error lies between particular limits is represented by the portion of area under the Law-of-Error curve between those limits relative to the whole area (which is unity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although any exact error value has infinitesimal probability in a continuous law, finite probabilities exist for intervals. Use areas under the curve to compute cumulative probabilities (e.g., probability error ≤ 3 inches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean is the most probable result (subject to assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean (arithmetical mean) is the most probable approximation to the true value when there is no knowledge contradicting the assumption that unknown causes of error are as likely to act one way as the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware some writers distinguish the 'mean' and the 'method of least squares,' but in single-variable cases they coincide. However, if there is known one-sided tendency or systematic bias, choosing the mean ignores that knowledge and may be inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for treating a mean result (eight-step procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A step-by-step arithmetic procedure to assess trustworthiness of a mean: 1) compute mean of observations; 2) find each observation's deviation from mean; 3) square these deviations; 4) sum the squares; 5) divide by (n − 1) to get the square of the mean error of a single observation; 6) take square root to get mean error of single observation; 7) divide by sqrt(n) to get mean error of the mean; 8) multiply by the natural constant 0.6745 (≈0.674) to obtain the probable error of the mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with a five-measurement example yielding a probable error. The probable error means the limits within which it is as likely as not (odds 1:1) that the true value lies. Calculations need not be carried to high precision in ordinary cases; truncation of decimals is acceptable unless high precision is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable error concerns only random errors, not constant (systematic) errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The probable error quantifies uncertainty due to random errors that act as often positively as negatively; it takes no account of constant (systematic) errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus the true result may lie far outside the probable-error limits because of unrecognized systematic errors. Always consider potential constant errors separately (instrument drift, calibration biases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer instruments or methods that avoid sources of error over relying on averaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Any method of measurement known to avoid a source of error is preferred to methods that rely on probability to eliminate that error by averaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One good instrument is worth many indifferent ones. When a method avoids a known error source, it is better to use it than to rely on multiplication of observations. Use domain-specific knowledge to choose methods that minimize systematic biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect one-sided tendencies; do not blindly use the mean when bias exists
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is reason to believe a tendency to error in one direction (e.g., thermometer drift, barometer reading low), the mean will not correct it and is not the best estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases either correct for the known tendency, choose the instrument that avoids the bias (e.g., barometer giving highest reading), or prefer very careful single experiments over many careless repetitions. Example: thermometer readings rise with instrument age; barometers read low due to imperfect vacuum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of divergent or anomalous observations — investigate before rejecting
rubrics_metrics.description: Divergent observations should not be arbitrarily excluded; first attempt to discover causes, and exclude only when there is evidence of specific non-random error (misreading, transcription, instrument slip).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbitrary rejection invites bias or 'cooking' figures; divergent results might indicate real effects that overturn theory and deserve weight and further research. If divergence is explained (e.g., misreading, mistaking division marks), correct or exclude. When results diverge regularly, investigate systematic causes and introduce corrections experimentally if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pierce's criterion for rejecting doubtful observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations should be rejected when the probability of the system of errors obtained by retaining them is less than that of the system obtained by their rejection multiplied by the probability of making so many and no more abnormal observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a formal probabilistic test for rejecting outliers; implemented and discussed in Chauvenet's manual. Use probabilistic reasoning (not arbitrary choice) to justify exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot distribution of apparent errors to check the Law of Error
rubrics_metrics.description: When observations are numerous, project the apparent errors into a curve and see if it exhibits the symmetrical characteristic form of the theoretical curve of error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the empirical curve matches the theoretical symmetric shape, infer errors arise from many small independent sources and compensate in the mean. Considerable irregularity indicates one-sided or large causes that need investigation. Use empirical comparison (Encke, Quetelet examples) to test adequacy of the law; note theory may under- or over-estimate large errors in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Least Squares for systems with multiple unknowns
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more unknown quantities must be determined simultaneously, use the Method of Least Squares to obtain the most probable values by forming and solving mean equations derived from many observation-equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: from observation equations ax + by = c, multiply each equation by coefficients, sum similar terms to form mean equations (sum of a^2 · x + sum of ab · y = sum of ac, etc.). Repeat for other coefficients for additional unknowns. Solve the resulting mean equations algebraically to get probable values. Computations are approximate; decimal places may be truncated to save work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special handling for gross integral deviations (transcription/instrument mistakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Very large integer discrepancies (e.g., off by a degree or half-degree) in astronomical reductions are often due to misreading or mistaken division marks and should be corrected or struck out rather than trusted to averaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such errors could not plausibly arise from observational or instrumental irregularity; correcting them or excluding obviously erroneous data is justified. When possible, obtain new observations instead of relying on dubious data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of scale-mismatch or trending sequences where mean is inappropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not take the mean of quantities that differ by very large factors or where measurements show a monotonic trend toward an extreme limit; domain knowledge may indicate a different best estimate than the arithmetic mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: historical estimates of stellar apparent diameters monotonically decreased as observational power increased; choosing the smallest estimate or another domain-informed estimator may be better than the arithmetic mean. Use knowledge of experimental improvements and systematic tendencies to choose appropriate aggregating methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical verification of theoretical error laws is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Law of Error follows logically from counting/permutations principles and the assumption of many independent small causes, it should be checked by comparing large series of observations with theoretical expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Encke and Quetelet compared observed frequency distributions of astronomical errors with theoretical curves — correspondence is generally close though deviations occur for large errors. Use empirical checks to judge applicability and to detect systematic departures.
